responses.markdown:
## Summary of action
Start a short, consistent sleep window and simple bedroom rules (limit time in bed to ~5 hours at first, fixed wake time every day, leave bed if not asleep after 20 minutes), add a 30–60 minute wind‑down with 10 minutes of paced breathing each night, avoid late caffeine and big meals, consider head‑of‑bed elevation for reflux, and aim for modest weight loss and asthma/GERD symptom control while you track sleep for 2–4 weeks.

## What your sleep points to
Your overnight study showed total sleep time 269.5 minutes (4.5 h), time in bed 482.5 minutes, sleep efficiency 55.9% (poor), no REM sleep detected, deep sleep (N3) proportion high at 35.8% of TST, and AHI 14.7 events/hour (mild). Watch for **Insomnia** (persistent difficulty falling or staying asleep), **Sleep disorders** (abnormal sleep architecture including absent REM), **Obesity** (which can fragment sleep and reduce sleep quality), and **Anxiety disorder** (nighttime worry that can maintain wakefulness).

## How the plan addresses these
Limiting time in bed initially to about 5.0 hours (bedtime set so you get a fixed wake time) concentrates sleep and raises sleep efficiency; leaving bed after ~20 minutes awake and returning only when sleepy strengthens the bed–sleep link. A nightly 30–60 minute wind‑down that ends with 10 minutes of slow diaphragmatic breathing helps reduce pre‑sleep arousal; stop caffeine after mid‑afternoon, avoid naps longer than 30 minutes and stop large meals 2–3 hours before bed, and elevate the head of the bed if reflux wakes you. Work with your clinician to ensure night asthma/GERD meds are optimised and to set a modest weight‑loss goal (for example 0.5–1 kg/week) as that often improves sleep. Keep a daily sleep diary for 2–4 weeks; if no clear improvement or daytime sleepiness persists, discuss further testing and treatment options. Behavioral sleep scheduling and stimulus-control measures are effective first-line strategies for chronic poor sleep [1][2].

References
1. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Chronic Insomnia: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis — PubMed 2015. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26054060/ [1]
2. Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine systematic review, meta-analysis, and GRADE assessment — PubMed 2021. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33164741/ [2]
